name: potential (can do)
english: Says someone can or can't do something.
use: The everyday way to say can and can't: nihongo hanaseru?, ashita ikeru?, mou taberarenai.
formation: Godan: change the final -u to -eru (kau → kaeru, iku → ikeru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -rareru (taberareru); in speech often just -reru (tabereru). suru → dekiru, kuru → korareru.

example.ja: 日本語、ちょっと話せるよ
example.english: I can speak a little Japanese.

examplePolite.ja: 日本語が少し話せます
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little Japanese.

notes: Ichidan potential sounds the same as the passive (taberareru, mirareru); context tells. kaeru 'can buy' also sounds like kaeru 'go home'.

name: passive
english: Something is done to someone, often with a feeling of 'it happened to me'.
use: Mostly for things done to you, often unwelcome: okorareta (I got told off), ame ni furareta (I got caught in the rain). At work the same form is also a light honorific (nanji ni kaeraremasu ka).
formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -reru (kau → kawareru, matsu → matareru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -rareru (taberareru). suru → sareru, kuru → korareru.

example.ja: 昨日部長に怒られた
example.english: I got chewed out by my boss yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日部長に怒られました
examplePolite.english: I got scolded by my manager yesterday.

notes: The person who does it to you takes ni (buchou ni). Ichidan passive and potential sound the same: mirareru = 'be seen' or 'can see'.

name: causative (make / let)
english: Makes or lets someone do something.
use: Heard most as -sasete or -sasete kudasai, 'let me': chotto kangaesasete (let me think). Also for a parent or boss making someone do something.
formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -seru (kau → kawaseru, matsu → mataseru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -saseru (tabesaseru). suru → saseru, kuru → kosaseru; the table shows the -te form (-sasete).

example.romaji: kondo wa watashi ni harawasete yo
example.ja: 今度は私に払わせてよ
example.english: Let me pay next time.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo wa watashi ni harawasete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: 今度は私に払わせてください
examplePolite.english: Please let me pay next time.

notes: -sasete kudasai asks to do it yourself; -te kudasai asks the other person to do it (harawasete = let me pay, haratte = you pay).

name: causative-passive (be made to)
english: Being made to do something you didn't want to.
use: For complaining about being forced or kept: nomasareta (they made me drink), matasareta (I was kept waiting).
formation: Godan: change the final -u to -a and add -sareru (kau → kawasareru, matsu → matasareru); verbs in -su use -saserareru (hanasaserareru). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -saserareru (tabesaserareru). suru → saserareru, kuru → kosaserareru.

example.ja: 昨日も三時間待たされたよ
example.english: I got kept waiting three hours again yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日も三時間待たされました
examplePolite.english: I was kept waiting three hours again yesterday.

notes: Listen for the extra -sa-: nomasareta = I was made to drink; nomareta = someone drank it (on me).

name: command form
english: A blunt order: do it!
use: Heard in anger, among rough-talking male friends, in sports cheering and on signs. Learners mostly need to recognise it; ganbare (go for it!) and chotto mate (hang on) are the friendly exceptions.
formation: Godan: change the final -u to -e (kau → kae, iku → ike). Ichidan: drop -ru, add -ro (tabero, miro). suru → shiro, kuru → koi.

example.ja: おい、早くしろよ
example.english: Hey, hurry up!

examplePolite.ja: すみません、早くしてください

notes: The command ike (go!) and the potential ikeru (can go) share the -e sound; the bare -e at the end is the order.

name: don't! (blunt)
english: A blunt 'don't!'.
use: Strong bans: parents to small kids, rough friends, signs and warnings. In normal talk people say -naide (sawaranaide).
formation: Dictionary form + na, for every verb: taberu na, iku na, suru na, kuru na.

example.ja: 危ない!それ触るな!
example.english: Careful! Don't touch that!

examplePolite.ja: 危ないですから、触らないでください
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous, so please don't touch it.

notes: Only a bare verb + na is a ban; na after other words is the feeling particle (ii na = that's nice).

name: -nasai command
english: A firm instruction, the way a parent or teacher gives it.
use: Parents to kids, teachers to students: hayaku nenasai, chanto tabenasai. It also lives in set phrases: gomennasai, okaerinasai, oyasuminasai.
formation: Use the -masu stem + nasai. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabenasai). Godan: change the final -u to -i (kainasai, machinasai, hanashinasai). suru → shinasai, kuru → kinasai.

example.ja: もう遅いから、早く寝なさい
example.english: It's late, go to bed now.

examplePolite.romaji: mou osoi desu kara, hayaku nete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: もう遅いですから、早く寝てください
examplePolite.english: It's late, so please go to bed.

notes: It sounds gentle but talks down; don't use it to adults you don't know.

name: blunt request
english: Do it (for me): a blunt request.
use: Mostly men, to friends or juniors, or in tense moments: matte kure! Everyday requests use just -te (matte) or -te kureru? (matte kureru?).
formation: te-form + kure: tabete kure, matte kure, nonde kure, shite kure, kite kure.

example.romaji: chotto matte kure, sugu iku kara
example.ja: ちょっと待ってくれ、すぐ行くから
example.english: Hang on, I'll be right there.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, sugu ikimasu kara
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、すぐ行きますから
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, please. I'll be right there.

notes: -te kure is an order; -te kureru? is a friendly question. Same verb, very different tone.

name: end up / finish (-chau)
english: Did it completely, or did it by accident and regret it.
use: All over casual talk, mostly in the past: tabechatta (I ate it all), wasurechatta (oops, I forgot). The full -te shimau is for more careful speech.
formation: Take the te-form: -te becomes -chau, -de becomes -jau (tabechau, katchau, nonjau). suru → shichau, kuru → kichau. Past: -chatta / -jatta.

example.ja: あ、傘電車に忘れちゃった
example.english: Oh no, I left my umbrella on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o densha ni wasurete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 傘を電車に忘れてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I left my umbrella on the train.

notes: -chatta is past (did it, oops); -chau is now or about to (I'll end up doing it).

name: do ahead (-toku)
english: Do it now, ready for later; or leave it as it is.
use: Planning and getting things ready: yoyaku shitoku ne (I'll book it). Also 'leave it': hottoite (leave me alone).
formation: Take the te-form: -te oku becomes -toku, -de oku becomes -doku (tabetoku, kattoku, nondoku). suru → shitoku, kuru → kitoku. Request: -toite / -doite.

example.ja: 店、予約しとくね
example.english: I'll book the restaurant.

examplePolite.romaji: omise o yoyaku shite okimasu ne
examplePolite.ja: お店を予約しておきますね
examplePolite.english: I'll book the restaurant ahead of time.

notes: -toku (do ahead) sounds close to -teku (-te iku, do before going): shitoku = I'll do it now for later; shiteku = I'll do it on my way.

name: try doing
english: Try doing it and see how it goes.
use: Suggesting or reporting a try: tabete mite (try it), itte mita (I went to check it out).
formation: te-form + miru: tabete miru, katte miru, nonde miru, shite miru, kite miru.

example.ja: これおいしいよ、食べてみて
example.english: This is good, try some.

examplePolite.romaji: kore oishii desu yo, tabete mite kudasai
examplePolite.ja: これおいしいですよ、食べてみてください
examplePolite.english: This is good, please try some.

notes: -te miru is 'try it and see'; -ou to suru is 'attempt it' (and maybe fail).

name: even if
english: Even if / even though.
use: For 'even if' and 'no matter what': ame futtemo iku. Also the start of asking permission: -temo ii? (is it OK if I...?).
formation: te-form + mo: tabetemo, kattemo, nondemo, shitemo, kitemo.

example.romaji: ame futtemo, ashita wa iku yo
example.ja: 雨降っても、明日は行くよ
example.english: Even if it rains, I'm going tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ame ga futtemo, ashita wa ikimasu
examplePolite.ja: 雨が降っても、明日は行きます
examplePolite.english: Even if it rains, I'll go tomorrow.

notes: After a verb, -demo is -te mo (nondemo = even if I drink), not the word demo 'but'.

name: things like (-tari)
english: Doing things like A and B, among other things.
use: Listing sample activities, usually closed with suru: eiga mitari, kaimono shitari shita. A single -tari keeps it vague (netari shite ta = I was sleeping and stuff).
formation: Past form + ri: tabetari, kattari, nondari, shitari, kitari. Close the list with suru (-tari -tari suru).

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa eiga mitari, kaimono shitari shita
example.ja: 週末は映画見たり、買い物したりした
example.english: At the weekend I watched movies, went shopping, that kind of thing.

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu wa eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 週末は映画を見たり、買い物をしたりしました
examplePolite.english: At the weekend I watched movies and went shopping, among other things.

notes: -tari lists examples; -te strings actions in order (eiga mite, kaimono shita = watched a movie, then shopped).

name: while doing
english: Doing one thing while doing another (same person).
use: Two actions at once by one person: arukinagara, terebi minagara. The main action comes last.
formation: -masu stem + nagara. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabenagara). Godan: change the final -u to -i (nominagara, hanashinagara). suru → shinagara, kuru → kinagara.

example.ja: いつもテレビ見ながらご飯食べてる
example.english: I always eat while watching TV.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo terebi o minagara gohan o tabemasu
examplePolite.ja: いつもテレビを見ながらご飯を食べます
examplePolite.english: I always eat while watching TV.

notes: Only for one person doing both. When someone else does the other thing, use -te iru aida (while they...).

name: without doing
english: Without doing it.
use: Doing one thing without the other: nani mo iwazu ni kaetta. In chat -naide is more common; -zu ni turns up in stories and set phrases (wasurezu ni).
formation: Negative stem + zu ni. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabezu ni). Godan: change the final -u to -a (kawazu ni, ikazu ni). suru → sezu ni, kuru → kozu ni.

example.ja: 何も言わずに帰っちゃった
example.english: He went home without saying anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nani mo iwazu ni kaette shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 何も言わずに帰ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: He went home without saying a word.

notes: suru becomes sezu ni, not shizu ni. -naide means the same and is the everyday choice (tabenaide).

name: looks about to
english: Looks like it's about to happen.
use: Judging from what you see: ame furisou (looks like rain), nakisou (about to cry), ochisou (about to fall).
formation: -masu stem + sou. Ichidan: drop -ru (tabesou). Godan: change the final -u to -i (furisou, nomisou). suru → shisou, kuru → kisou.

example.ja: 空暗いね、雨降りそう
example.english: The sky's dark. Looks like rain.

examplePolite.english: It looks like it's going to rain.

notes: Stem + sou = 'looks like'; dictionary form + sou da = 'I hear' (furu sou da = I hear it'll rain).

name: too much
english: Doing something too much.
use: Mostly in the past, about overdoing it: tabesugita, nomisugita. Works on adjectives too: takasugiru (too expensive).
formation: -masu stem + sugiru: tabesugiru, nomisugiru, hanashisugiru, shisugiru, kisugiru. Adjectives drop -i (takasugiru; ii → yosugiru). It then conjugates like an ichidan verb (tabesugita).

example.ja: 昨日飲みすぎて、頭痛い
example.english: I drank too much yesterday and my head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou nomisugite, atama ga itai desu
examplePolite.ja: 昨日飲みすぎて、頭が痛いです
examplePolite.english: I drank too much yesterday, so I have a headache.

notes: -sugi on its own is a casual exclamation: kawaisugi! (way too cute), not a mistake.

name: easy / hard to do
english: Easy to do / hard to do.
use: Describing things and people: kono pen kakiyasui, hanashiyasui hito. -yasui also means 'tends to': kaze hikiyasui.
formation: -masu stem + yasui or nikui: tabeyasui, kaiyasui, hanashiyasui, shiyasui, kiyasui. The result acts like an i-adjective (tabeyasukatta, wakarinikui).

example.ja: この靴、すごく歩きやすいよ
example.english: These shoes are really easy to walk in.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa totemo arukiyasui desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はとても歩きやすいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are very easy to walk in.

notes: -yasui after a verb stem is 'easy to', not yasui 'cheap'.

name: spoken -nnai
english: In fast speech, -ranai and -ru before n turn into n.
use: All over casual speech, so you mostly need to hear it: wakannai (I don't get it), tsumannai (boring), shiran (dunno).
formation: Before n, a verb's r-sound becomes n: kaeranai → kaennai, wakaranai → wakannai, nani shiteru no → nani shiten no. In rough or western speech -nai can shrink to -n: shiranai → shiran.

example.ja: 何言ってるか全然わかんない
example.english: I have no idea what he's saying.

notes: The doubled n is the whole clue: wakannai is just wakaranai, not a different word.

name: spoken contractions
english: The squeezed sounds of fast casual speech.
use: Nearly every casual sentence has one; learn to hear each as its full form. Using them with friends sounds natural.
formation: -nakereba → -nakya, as in the table (tabenakya, ikanakya, konakya). Also -te iru → -teru, -te oku → -toku, -te shimau → -chau, -te wa → -cha, -te iku → -teku. And de wa → ja, no da → n da, -eba → -ya (ikeba → ikya).

example.romaji: gomen, mou kaeranakya. ashita hayai n da
example.ja: ごめん、もう帰らなきゃ。明日早いんだ
example.english: Sorry, I've got to head home. Early start tomorrow.

notes: -cha and -chau differ by one sound: tabecha dame = you can't eat it; tabechau = I'll eat it all up.
